title: Isandro and the Lantern
premise: In 1847, Rosalind Amberdale, daughter of a drowned pearl diver, works off her family's debt as an indentured clerk at the Corvane Trading Company on the frozen edge of the river port of Hallowmere. When an infant is abandoned at the company door with a note reading 'forget this face,' Rosalind secretly takes the child in, hiding her among the lantern-lit storerooms. As spring approaches and the ice begins to crack, the company orders the last river berth — the only passage out before the flood season seals the town for months — to be filled by a single passenger. Rosalind must choose between sending her ailing younger brother Tam to safety with relatives upriver or keeping the berth for herself and the foundling whose face someone powerful wants forgotten. She gives the berth to Tam, exposes the child's parentage — the illegitimate granddaughter of the company's own director — and in doing so loses her indenture but gains an unlikely family: the cook Marta, the lamplighter Isandro (for whom the child is named), and a future built not on survival alone but on belonging.
about_author: Wendell Montrose is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing shipping ledgers from nineteenth-century river ports. Their fiction draws on the marginalia of those records — the names scrawled in margins by people history nearly forgot.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Hands
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. We meet her at sixteen, tallying cargo in the Corvane warehouse, invisible by design since her father drowned in debt. She memorizes rules: don't speak first, don't want loudly. Emotional beat: quiet resignation masking a fierce, buried hope.

chapters.title: Ledgers and Lanterns
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She describes the nightly ritual of lighting the storeroom lanterns with Isandro, the old lamplighter who treats her like a niece. Her brother Tam coughs through the winter; the company doctor costs more than they have. Beat: warmth against cold, family made of habit.

chapters.title: A Bundle at the Door
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. During a whiteout night, she finds an infant on the loading dock with a note: 'Forget this face.' No name, no claimant. Instead of reporting it, she carries the child inside. Beat: terror and a sudden, irreversible tenderness.

chapters.title: Rules of Invisibility
chapters.summary: Marta the cook's POV. Marta discovers the baby but chooses silence, teaching Rosalind how to feed and hide her. The two women form a conspiracy of care. Beat: complicity as intimacy; the found family begins forming around the child.

chapters.title: The Director's Winter Visit
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Director Ambrose Corvane arrives to inspect accounts, cold-eyed and exacting. Rosalind notices he lingers near the dock where the baby was left, asking odd questions about that night. Beat: dread creeping into ordinary work.

chapters.title: What Tam Remembers
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Bedridden, Tam recalls their mother's stories of their father's final dive and the debt that bound them. He suspects Rosalind is hiding something and keeps her secret without being asked. Beat: sibling loyalty as quiet heroism.

chapters.title: Naming the Nameless
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Isandro helps Rosalind christen the baby 'Lantern' in jest, then seriously — a small ceremony in the lamp room. He reveals he once lost a daughter to the river. Beat: grief transmuted into guardianship.

chapters.title: The Berth Announcement
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Spring notices arrive: when the ice breaks, one passenger berth will be granted on the last boat before flood season closes Hallowmere for months. Company employees may petition. Beat: hope and arithmetic — one berth, three candidates.

chapters.title: Petitions and Prices
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. Marta urges Rosalind to take the berth herself and leave the company forever. Rosalind calculates what leaving means: abandoning Tam, abandoning Lantern. Beat: the price of survival made explicit.

chapters.title: A Face in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Digging through old shipping records, Rosalind finds a birth entry matching the baby's blanket embroidery — the director's late son and a laundress. The child is a Corvane. Beat: revelation that turns hiding into leverage and danger.

chapters.title: The Watchman's Question
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. A hired watchman, Mr. Quill, begins searching the premises for 'company property gone missing.' Isandro misdirects him but is marked. Beat: the noose tightening; loyalty tested under surveillance.

chapters.title: Tam Worsens
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Tam's fever spikes; the doctor says river air upriver could save him — if he travels before the ice breaks. Suddenly the berth is not ambition but medicine. Beat: stakes crystallize into a body, a breath, a deadline.

chapters.title: Bargaining with Corvane
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind petitions the director for Tam's berth and glimpses genuine grief flicker behind his authority. He neither grants nor refuses, telling her the ice will decide. Beat: seeing the enemy as a wounded man; moral complexity.

chapters.title: Quill Closes In
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. Quill searches the kitchen; Lantern nearly cries. Marta burns the embroidered blanket to destroy evidence, weeping over the loss. Beat: sacrifice of memory for safety; the cost compounds.

chapters.title: The Ice Begins to Sing
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The river groans and cracks — days remain. Isandro offers to flee with Lantern, but Rosalind realizes flight means the child grows up hunted and nameless. Beat: the choice reframed from escape to confrontation.

chapters.title: A Letter Never Sent
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind finds the director's unsent letter to his dead son, confessing shame. She understands: he ordered the child forgotten to protect his name, not from cruelty. Beat: empathy as strategy; she decides to give him back his granddaughter.

chapters.title: The Last Berth
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. At the manifest signing, Rosalind surrenders her own petition and places Tam's name — then watches the director add a second line himself: passage for the child, unrecorded but undeniable. Beat: climax of mercy; the choice made and honored.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Dock
chapters.summary: Quill's POV. Quill attempts to seize the baby at departure; Rosalind publicly names the child's parentage before the assembled crew. The director silences Quill with a single word. Beat: exposure as salvation; invisibility finally discarded.

chapters.title: Breaking
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven. The ice breaks; the boat pulls away with Tam waving, Lantern held by the director's housekeeper, Rosalind ashore. Grief and relief collide. Beat: letting go as the truest act of family.

chapters.title: After the Flood
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. Flood season passes; the town rebuilds. Rosalind's indenture is voided — the director calls it severance, everyone knows it's gratitude. She stays, unemployed and free. Beat: disorientation of freedom after survival.

chapters.title: The Lamp Room
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Isandro formally teaches Rosalind the lamplighter's rounds; she becomes his apprentice and heir to the route. Lantern visits on Sundays, called by her true name now: Isandra. Beat: inheritance chosen rather than owed.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. One year later, Rosalind writes her father's name into the ledger margin where history forgot it, then closes the book. Tam letters home; Lantern laughs in the doorway. Beat: resolution — belonging is not given or survived, but built, lit nightly like a lamp.
